answers.text: Three lines, same order every time: delivery date, item and quantity, any change from the original order. That's the whole trick, keeping it fixed.
Everyone runs the week's claims through the same instruction: list each claim by date, amount, category and submitter, then total it up at the bottom.
The dates don't line up — 'three days out from today' against the revised delivery date on the 19th feels wrong. Worth checking the actual call date before it's sent.
62 up from 54 is about right for 15%. The on-time rate looks off though — 3 late out of 62 isn't 97%. I'd flag it.
Output 2 every time — you can see the €612,000 and €25,100 behind the 4.1%. Output 1 gives you nothing to check.
Reply 2 — it has the order and credit references so it's traceable. Reply 1 sounds sincere but there's nothing to look up.
1. No. 2. Yes. 3. No. 4. Yes, it's already public. 5. No.
I'd keep the pricing and confidentiality details out of an unvetted tool — those feel like the risky parts of the contract.
I'd cross-check the report totals against the warehouse system before it goes to the manager — a two-minute step, not a full re-read.
Step 1, where the AI reads the order, is the one I'd watch most closely.
